newsitem.title: USA: AMR pilots' union sees 50 pct strike chance.
newsitem.headline: AMR pilots' union sees 50 pct strike chance.

text.p: Union leaders representing the pilots of AMR Corp's American Airlines see a 50 percent possibility of their labor dispute ending in a mid-February strike, a senior union official said.
"It is something we certainly don't want but there is a good chance ... Fifty-fifty is a good probability," the official said, asking not to be identified.
The same message was given to members of the Allied Pilots Association at a closed-doors union meeting in Dallas on Thursday morning.

"We have at least a 50 percent probability of having to strike the airline. It is the last thing I want in the world to see happen, but we should be prepared," a member of the union's newly-elected negotiating committee told the meeting.

American Airlines and the APA on Wednesday turned down the offer of binding arbitration and were immediately placed by the National Mediation Board in a 30-day "cooling off" period which could lead to a strike or a lockout starting Feb. 15.
Union officials on Thursday stepped up preparations for a possible strike but said they would rather reach a negotiated settlement during the 30-day cooling off period.
"We are absolutely serious about that. If management is serious, let's do it. Why should we wait until the airline loses $500 million in advanced bookings?" the official said.
He said the probability of a strike would rise steadily the further the two sides went into the 30-day cooling off period.
Union members last week rejected a tentative four-year labor contract which APA leaders had agreed to last September, and have since drawn up a list of fresh demands.

They include pay raises of more than 11 percent over the next four years, options on 7.25 million company shares at a discount of $10 each, elimination of a two-tier pay structure and a guarantee that American will not use its commuter carrier American Eagle to fly 50-passenger regional jets.
AMR management says the demands would cripple the airline's ability to compete and threaten its growth plans, including a $6.5 billion contract to buy 103 jets from Boeing Co.
